content:
I was looking at the documentation for Mathlib/Algebra/Module/Defs, and it seems that Module.ext and Module.ext_iff and Module.toMulActionWithZero have strangely named "instances":
{inst✝ : Semiring R} {inst✝¹ : AddCommMonoid M}
or
{x✝ : Semiring R} {x✝¹ : AddCommMonoid M}
I don't see why they are written this way—especially since the ✝ symbol is usually untypable. It seems that [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] would have worked too. Is this intentional, or should these be changed to match the conventions for the rest of the page?
I see exactly what you say "would have worked" in the code. Maybe you're confusing the code and the generated documentation?

That's a good point. I guess the source code is a bit more complicated. Firstly, Module.toMulActionWithZero seems unusual since it does have {_ : Semiring R}:

instance (priority := 100) Module.toMulActionWithZero
    {R M} {_ : Semiring R} {_ : AddCommMonoid M} [Module R M] : MulActionWithZero R M := …

Meanwhile, I'm not sure why the other two theorems have the generated instances. I'm looking for another example to compare it to
Apparently it was intentional for performance reason https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/17582
And it is probably a good idea to try undoing the change now and see if Lean is smarter

Danny said:

Meanwhile, I'm not sure why the other two theorems have the generated instances. I'm looking for another example to compare it to

I'm having difficulty finding any other examples where @[ext] is called on a class. I keep finding structure or def instead of class. I'm also searching without a particular strategy other than looking for definitions that would require a similar context to that used to define Module.
I wasn't able to find any other examples

The reason is indeed performance, in particular this affects the synthesis order. When the instance is written like this, that means that during type class search, when it is applied to a goal MulActionWithZero R M, it will then only generate the subgoal Module R M, and the Semiring R and AddCommMonoid M instances will then be filled in implicitly as a result. This is faster than first searching for Semiring R and AddCommMonoid M separately.

I heard that the FRO is planning to improve some performance aspects of type class search. I wonder if that includes improvements to the synth order.
